issues.legal_issue: A grant to harvest forest produce is a licence rather than a lease when it confers no interest in or exclusive possession of the land and entry onto the land is merely ancillary to harvesting.
material_facts: The agreements ran for nine to ten months and created no estate or interest in the land.
The grantees received no exclusive possession or control of the land, but only the right to pluck, cut, carry away and appropriate forest produce existing or arising during the agreement period.
The right to enter the land was ancillary to harvesting the forest produce.
issues.conclusion: The agreements were licences, not leases, and did not attract stamp duty applicable to leases under Article 31(c).
issues.legal_principle: Under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers a right to enjoy immovable property; under section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, a licence permits an act on another’s property without creating an interest in it. The definitions of immovable property in section 3(26) of the General Clauses Act, section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 2(6) of the Registration Act support the distinction. The substance and essence of the agreement, rather than its form, and the parties’ intention determine its character; an interest in the property indicates a lease, whereas permission to use the property while possession remains with the owner indicates a licence. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, Kauri Timber Company Limited v. Commissioner of Taxes, Marshall v. Green and Firm Chhotabhai Jethabai Patel & Co. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and distinguished Mahadeo v. State of Bombay. Article 31(c) of the Stamp Act was therefore inapplicable.

rule.if: forest_produce_harvesting_grant and short_term_grant and no_land_interest_created and no_exclusive_land_possession and land_entry_is_ancillary and stamp_duty_classification_dispute

predicates.forest_produce_harvesting_grant: A grant gives the recipient rights to harvest and take away forest produce.
predicates.short_term_grant: The grant is for a short period.
predicates.no_land_interest_created: The agreement creates no estate or other interest in the land.
predicates.no_exclusive_land_possession: The recipient is not given exclusive possession or control of the land.
predicates.land_entry_is_ancillary: Entry onto the land is only incidental to the purpose of harvesting the produce.
predicates.stamp_duty_classification_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an agreement is a lease or licence for stamp-duty purposes.

issues.definition: When a short-term forest-produce harvesting grant creates no land interest or exclusive possession and access is only ancillary, a stamp-duty classification dispute results in the grant being treated as a licence rather than a lease.

issues.legal_issue: A government’s annual auction of forest produce does not by itself establish that it carries on the business of selling that class of goods for sales-tax liability.
material_facts: The forest department sold forest produce by auction only annually, rather than at frequent intervals.
The respondents were required by the sale notice to pay sales tax on their bid amounts.
The evidence did not establish the frequency of sales transactions necessary to show that the government carried on the business of selling forest produce.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were not liable to pay sales tax on their bid amounts because the government was not shown to carry on the business of selling forest produce.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5, 2(e), 2(bbb) and 2(n) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, respectively address the levy, dealer, business and sale. To impose the tax in these circumstances, the government had to be carrying on the business of selling the forest produce. Following State of Gujarat v. Raipur Manufacturing Co. Ltd., the Court considered the volume, frequency, continuity and regularity of transactions; after the 1966 amendment, profit motive was not essential. The lack of frequent transactions, since auctions occurred only annually, meant that the government was not carrying on that business. The Court also referred to P.T.C.C.S. Merchants Union v. State of A.P., Raja Bhairabendra v. Superintendent of Taxes, Orient Paper Mills Ltd. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Deputy Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax and Sales Tax, Quilon v. Travancore Rubber and Tea Co., Deputy Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax and Sales Tax, Quilon v. Midland Rubber and Produce Co. Ltd., and Ramakrishna Deo v. Collector of Sales Tax, Orissa.

rule.if: sales_tax_liability_dispute and government_sells_forest_produce and auctions_are_only_annual and frequent_sales_transactions_not_established

predicates.sales_tax_liability_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether purchasers must pay sales tax on amounts bid for goods.
predicates.government_sells_forest_produce: A government sells forest produce to purchasers.
predicates.auctions_are_only_annual: The government holds the relevant auctions only once each year.
predicates.frequent_sales_transactions_not_establis: The evidence does not establish frequent sales transactions by the government.

issues.definition: When a sales-tax liability dispute concerns government sales of forest produce made only through annual auctions, and frequent sales transactions are not established, the purchasers are not liable for sales tax.

issues.legal_issue: A security deposit is not a mortgage instrument for stamp-duty purposes unless the instrument creates a right in specified property in favour of another person to secure an obligation.
material_facts: The sale notice provided for earnest-money deposits to be returned to unsuccessful bidders when the sales concluded, while permitting retention of a bidder’s deposit in specified circumstances.
The clause relied on did not create any right in or over the security deposits in favour of the government.
The respondents were nevertheless demanded stamp duty on their security deposits as if they were mortgages.
issues.conclusion: The security deposits were not mortgage deeds and were not chargeable to stamp duty under Article 35(c).
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(17) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 defines a mortgage deed to include an instrument that, to secure money advanced or to be advanced, a debt, or performance of an engagement, transfers or creates in favour of another a right over or in respect of specified property. The instrument must create such a right in specified property. The Court approved Reference under Stamp Act, Section 46 and Rishidev Sondhi v. Dhampur Sugar Mills, which support the requirement that an interest in the deposit be created; merely identifying money as security does not suffice. Article 35(c) was therefore inapplicable.

predicates.stamp_duty_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument attracts stamp duty as a mortgage deed.
predicates.security_deposit_given: A party gives a deposit to secure performance of an obligation.
predicates.instrument_creates_no_right_in_deposit: The instrument does not create a right in or over the deposit in favour of the person receiving it.

issues.definition: When a stamp-duty classification dispute concerns a security deposit and the instrument creates no right in or over that deposit, the deposit instrument is not a mortgage instrument.
